findings.title: Advertising tracker fires before any consent interaction
findings.rationale_plain: Advertising trackers collect a persistent browser identifier, your IP address and the pages you visit, and send them to a company that uses them for its own purposes. Under DPDP that is processing of personal data. It needs your consent, and consent has to come before the processing starts, not after.
findings.rationale_dev: A request to a C6 vendor was observed before any consent banner was detected (or before any interaction, once interaction scans are enabled). s.6(1) requires a clear affirmative act before processing; s.5(1) requires notice to precede or accompany the consent request. Firing on page load satisfies neither. The vendor is an independent or joint Data Fiduciary for this disclosure (s.2(i)), so s.11(1)(b) also requires it to be named.
findings.remediation_summary: Gate the tag behind a consent signal so it does not load until an affirmative act is recorded.

findings.title: Banner has an accept control but no equivalent reject control
findings.rationale_plain: Consent must be free and unconditional, and withdrawal must be as easy as giving consent. A banner that makes accepting one click and rejecting several clicks — or impossible — does not produce free consent.
findings.rationale_dev: The banner exposes an accept control but no reject control. s.6(1) requires consent to be "free … unconditional"; s.6(4) requires withdrawal with ease comparable to giving. An asymmetric banner fails both.
findings.remediation_summary: Add a reject control of equal prominence to the accept control.

findings.title: Session replay or heatmap tool fires before consent
findings.rationale_plain: Session replay and heatmap tools record what you do on a page — mouse movements, clicks, keystrokes, the page content itself. That is behavioural monitoring. Under DPDP it needs consent, and where children are reachable it is prohibited outright regardless of consent.
findings.rationale_dev: A request to a C5 (session replay / heatmap) vendor was observed before any consent banner was detected. s.6(1) requires a clear affirmative act before processing. Where the site plausibly reaches under-18s, s.9(3) prohibits behavioural monitoring entirely (see DPDP-C-040).
findings.remediation_summary: Gate the session-replay / heatmap tag behind a consent signal; on a site reaching minors, do not load it at all.

findings.title: No language option beyond English in the notice or banner
findings.rationale_plain: The Act requires that a person be given the option to access the notice in English or any of the 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule. A notice or banner offered only in English does not meet that requirement.
findings.rationale_dev: No language switcher was detected on the banner and the page language is English. s.5(3) and s.6(3) require the option of English or any Eighth Schedule language. This is a heuristic — a site may offer language choice elsewhere — so detection confidence is marked accordingly and the finding is phrased as "we could not find".
findings.remediation_summary: Offer the notice in English plus at least the relevant Eighth Schedule languages, with a visible language control.

findings.title: Session replay or heatmap tool present at all
findings.rationale_plain: A session replay or heatmap tool is present on the page. Behavioural monitoring requires consent under DPDP. Its presence does not by itself prove a breach — it may be consent-gated — but it is the category of processing that most often runs without valid consent and is prohibited outright where children are reachable.
findings.rationale_dev: A request to a C5 vendor was observed. Behavioural monitoring requires consent (s.6(1)); where children are reachable it is prohibited regardless of consent (s.9(3), see DPDP-C-040). This finding flags presence; the pre-consent variant is DPDP-C-007.
findings.remediation_summary: Confirm the tool is consent-gated and does not record before the affirmative act; mask sensitive fields by default.

findings.title: Third-party endpoint resolves outside India (permitted by default)
findings.rationale_plain: A third-party endpoint resolves outside India. This is NOT a contravention: s.16 permits the transfer of personal data outside India unless the destination is notified by the Central Government. The rule is tiered open only because the criteria for "Significant Data Fiduciary" designation — under which Rule 13(4) localisation may bite — are not yet specified. This rule exists to correct the GDPR-trained assumption that cross-border transfer is automatically a problem; under DPDP it is permitted by default.
findings.rationale_dev: Detection: a third-party request whose resolved destination_country is not "IN". Resolution prefers the engine's request.destination_country, then the tracker dataset's destination_countries[0]. The finding is informational — it carries the note that transfer is permitted unless the destination is notified. It becomes legally live only if the Data Fiduciary is later designated an SDF.
findings.remediation_summary: None required by default. If the Data Fiduciary is or may be designated a Significant Data Fiduciary, assess Rule 13(4) localisation before transfer.

questions.title: Behavioural tracking or targeted advertising on a site plausibly reaching under-18s
questions.prompt: Does this site reach people under 18?
questions.consequence_if_true: If this site reaches under-18s, switch off C5 (behavioural monitoring) and C6 (targeted advertising) for those users; consent does not cure it.
questions.rationale_plain: Tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children are prohibited under DPDP, and consent cannot lift that prohibition. Whether a site reaches people under 18 is something a crawler cannot see — so this is a question for you, not a finding from the scan.

questions.title: Access logs as "traffic data" under the one-year retention floor
questions.prompt: Do your server access logs (which contain visitor IPs) fall under "traffic data" as the term is used in the DPDP Rules, and if so, is the one-year retention floor in Rule 8(3) being met? The term "traffic data" is not defined in the Act or Rules; the likely anchor is the IT Act s.69B regime.
questions.consequence_if_true: Confirm whether access logs are "traffic data"; if so, retain for at least one year per Rule 8(3) and document the basis.
questions.rationale_plain: Rule 8(3) imposes a one-year retention floor for "traffic data". The term is not defined in the Act or the Rules; the likely anchor is the IT Act s.69B regime. Whether server access logs (which contain visitor IP addresses) are "traffic data" is therefore an open question. This rule is unobservable from the page and is put to counsel as a question.

limits: Server-side tagging, backend relays, logs and retention are not observable by a crawler.
Consent-banner interaction was not performed; findings reflect the page state before any user action.
This is a reading of the DPDP Act and Rules, not legal advice and not a compliance verdict.
